SPECIAL MENTIONS 
Need to provide special package for development of NH-6 between 
Sambalpur and Bargarh in Orissa 
MS. PRAMILA BOHIDAR (Orissa): Mr. Chairman, Sir, all the 
National Highways are lifeline of the nation. They are like veins and arteries. It 
should be so in the case of NH-6 which passes through Sambalpur 
connecting Mumbai and Kolkata. 
NH-6, as on today, remains a two- lane way, even though it goes 
through the densest industrial and agricultural belt in Orissa. 
Between Bargarh and Sambalpur, it serves the industrial towns of 
Bargarh, Burla, Hirakud, Sambalpur and even the peripheral Jharsuguda-
Belpahar zone of the Mahanadi Coalfiel ds Ltd. (MCL). Needless to say, the 
mines and minerals, finished products like iron, aluminium, coal, etc. are 
carried through this National Highway. The Bargarh-Atabira belt is considered 
the rice bowl of Orissa and the FCI procures and stores paddy by hauling 
them through NH-6. 
Sambalpur-Hirakud-Burla areas house one university, one 
engineering and medical college each, apart from the Hirakud Irrigation Canal 
Systern, No wonder, the traffic on NH-6 is swelling and density of vehicles and 
road users is increasing day by day. Congestion on roads and causalities due 
to accidents are increasing. Most of the road accident victims on NH-6 
between Bargarh and Ainthapali Junction near Sambalpur are in the age 
group of 18-40, which is the most productive span in a man's lifetime. 
196 

[5 August, 2003] RAJYA SABHA 
The Minister for Road Transport and Highways had announced that 
Rs. 7.57 crores would be spent on improving the riding quality of roads in 
three phases between September 2002 and June 2003. I urge upon the hon. 
Minister to urgently take up four-laning of NH-6 between Sambalpur and 
Bargarh as a special package on priority basis during the current financial 
year so that trade and commerce can gr ow and precious lives are not lost 
further in gruesome road accidents. 
Need to ban wax coating on Fruits and Vegetables 
SHRI SANTOSH BAGRODIA (Rajasthan): Sir, as Shri Suresh 
Pachouri has just now talked about milk, I want to talk about fruits and 
vegetables. 
Whether the Government is willing to take the responsibility of health 
of crores of citizens is a big questi on. The use of wax by traders and vendors 
to polish fruits and vegetables to make them shining and attractive and 
preserving the moisture inside to minimize wastage and increase the profit 
are old practices and the Government has been aware of it for a long time. 
Edible wax is imported from U SA and other European countries and 
most of the vendors in Indi a are not in a position to import wax from these 
countries. Naturally, they would use the alternative wax which is commonly 
available in Indian markets. 
As stated by Shri S. R. Gupta, Director-General, PFA, there are two 
types of waxes, edible and non-edible. But in India, there is no guarantee that 
the correct one will be used and many people do not even wash or peel the 
fruits before eating. Even the Health Mi nistry believes that wax coating could 
be adulterated with chemicals harmful to health. However, the concept of 
fresh fruits and vegetables is liquidated by  the use of wax. Naturally, it is the 
health of crores of people that the Government should worry about rather than 
the handful who use it and make profit out of it. 
Therefore, I urge upon the Governm ent to immediately ban the use 
of wax on fruits and vegetables till some kind of a guarantee is given that only 
safe and edible wax would be used in future.

Need a for setting up of a regional centre of National Institute of Virology and

SHRIMATI N.P. DURGA (Andhra Pradesh): Sir, the recent 
mysterious viral fever, which baffled the scientists, doctors and experts even 
from the National Institute of Viro logy and the National Institute of 
Communicable Diseases, took its toll of  children, with low-resistance, in 
Andhra Pradesh. The scientists of NI V and NICD were perplexed and could 
not identify the inexplicable virus behind the viral fever in some districts of 
Andhra Pradesh, since the children, who were admitted in hospitals, were 
characterised by allergic rashes a nd high temperature of 105 degrees, then 
fits were caused by brain oedema, then they slipped into coma and died within 
hours. Even the epidemiological studies failed to identify the suspected viral 
encephalitis. Though the State Government , after making strenuous efforts, 
succeeded in controlling this menace, but  by that time, it had taken its. toll. 
The main problem is that the State Go vernment does not have the necessary 
expertise that the NIV and NICD have. The Government of Andhra Pradesh 
has given ex-gratia of Rs.50,000/-, asked the DG HS to go on leave and also 
suspended some health officials. But, all this does not solve the problem 
unless we have a regional centre of the National Institute of Virology and the 
National Institute of Communicable Diseases at Hyderabad so as to rush to 
the spot, whenever such unknown viral fever comes to light, not only in 
Andhra Pradesh but also in other Sout hern States, since this has become an 
event of every monsoon. The distance of above institutes also added more 
deaths since they had consumed more time in testing the blood strains of the 
victims. Hence, I strongly demand for est ablishment of the Regional Institutes 
of the National Institute of Virology and the National Institute of Communicable 
Diseases at Hyderabad immediately.

cultural identity is not threatened. We have the Special Marriage Act, 1954. It

deficit. Today, there is an answer to a similar question on the floor of the

fiscal deficit is quite alarming. Fiscal deficit is essentially a borrowing. We have

expenditure. This is a luxury which the country can't afford at this juncture. We 
have to come out of this situation. If the same trend continues, many social 
problems are sure to come. I don't want to be a Prophet of

DR. V. MAITREYAN (Tamil Nadu): Madam Deputy Chairperson, 
representing a regional party, especially the ruling party, I shall focus on the 
problems faced by us, what we have done in the last two years or so and what 
we expect from the Union Finance Minister. 
Since the mid 1990s, the public finances of Tamil Nadu have shown 
extremely disturbing trends. On the one hand, the revenue expenditure, 
comprising commitments on salaries, pensions, interest payments, subsidies 
and grants has shown a phenomenal increase. And, on the other, the revenue 
receipts did not keep pace with the unprecedented increase in the revenue 
expenditure, resulting in worsening the revenue deficit. Added to this, a higher 
level of borrowings, primarily intended to meet the revenue deficit, has added 
to the problem and has also led to a worsening of the fiscal deficit. 
242 

[5 August, 2003] RAJYA SABHA 
Following the recommendations of the Eleventh Finance 
Commission, Tamil Nadu's share in the divisible pool of Central Taxes is 
reduced by an estimated amount of Rs . 2,946 crores for the period 2000-
2005. Further, the Government of Indi a reduced its promised devolution of 
Central taxes by a further amount of Rs. 540 crores in 2001-2002, and Rs. 
274.50 crores in 2002-2003, due to poor collection of the Central taxes. This 
has further exacerbated the already worse financial situation. 
After the AIADMK Government, led by hon. Chief Mi nister, Dr. J. 
Jayalalithaaji, assumed office in May, 2001, we had undertaken a series of 
major fiscal reforms, covering the revenue expenditure as well as the revenue 
receipts of the State. Madam, under th e Chairmanship of Dr. Raja J. Chelliah, 
Tax Reforms and Revenue Augmentation Commission was constituted to 
increase the tax and non-tax revenues, and to streamline the tax 
administration system in the Stat e, and its interim report has been 
incorporated in the Budget for this y ear. The last year's Budget indicated an 
additional resource mobilization, throug h changes in taxation, of nearly Rs. 
690 crores and this has yielded very good results for us. 
The Samadhan Scheme, for settling th e stamp duty dues in disputed 
cases, has yielded additional revenue of Rs. 100 crores last year. Due to an 
intensive checking, enforcement and bette r collection, the Sales Tax, last 
year, has increased 15 per cent over t he previous year. This year's Budget 
provides for an additional resource mobilization of nearly Rs. 480 crores. Also, 
on non-tax side, such as forests, i rrigation, mines and minerals have all 
improved. With reference to revenue expenditure, as an economy measure, 
certain benefits to the Government Employees, such as encashment of leave, 
payment of bonus, etc., have been curtailed. The burden imposed by new 
instalments of Dearness Allowance has been handled by making the payment 
with a lag. The Government has constituted a Staff and Expenditure Reforms 
Commission, headed by Dr A.M. Swaminathan, a retired I.A.S. officer. Based 
on the identified surplus posts, abolit ion of equivalent posts is being 
undertaken. And, the Government has taken a committed decision that new 
recruitment in Government is totally banned with effect from November 2001, 
except a few essential categories such  as police, doctors and teachers. The 
Government has already announced a new Contributory Pension Scheme 
which will be applicable to selected categories of new employees who are 
employed w.e.f. 1st April, 2003. Also, other pension entitlements have been 
introduced 
243 

RAJYA SABHA [5 August, 2003] 
to contain the galloping pension costs.  One of the major focuses, towards 
which we have turned our attention during this period, is that we have 
undertaken a major restructuring of the food subsidy. The distribution of rice 
through fair price shops at Rs. 3.50 per  kg. resulted in a huge subsidy -bill of 
about Rs. 1500 crores per annum. With effect from 1 st October, 2002, the 
issue price of rice has been modified. The first 10 kgs would cost Rs. 3.50 kg., 
the next 10 kgs. would cost Rs. 6.00 per Kg. We have also decided to go in for 
a decentralised procurement, based on an  MoU with the Government of India. 
With these measures, the food subsidy burden will come down to Rs. 600 
crores, in 2003-04. This is a major re form measure that we have undertaken, 
after we have come to power. 
The Government has taken firm steps to restructure the public sector 
undertakings in Tamil Nadu. We have ordered for closure of eight public 
sector undertakings. A comprehensive voluntary retirement scheme has also 
been introduced with effect from May, 2002. We have announced a policy of 
exit from the manufacturing activi ties, undertaken by public sector 
undertakings and cooperative sector. A policy on disinvestment, consistent. 
with the policy adopted by the Government of India, has been formulated and 
will be pushed through in 2003-04. 
Another major area, where we have focused our attention, is the 
power sector reforms. The previous Government had constituted a State 
Electricity Regulatory Commission. But it was not made operational. The 
previous Government had also drawn fu nds from the Central Government in 
March, 2001, just prior to the Assembly elections, for which a Memorandum of 
Understanding was to be signed, which was not signed. After we have come 
to power, an agreement has been reach ed with the Central Government, with 
reference to the reforms to be undertaken in the power sector. Based on that, 
the State Electricity Regulatory Commission has, now, been made 
operational. The Tamil Nadu Electricity Board has applied for tariff revision 
before the Commission, as per the st ipulation, on the due date, the 30 th 
September, fast year. T he outstanding dues of Rs . 1,962 crores from the 
Tamil Nadu Electricity Board have been se curitized, as a one-time settlement 
of dues to central utilities. This has been taken over as debt by the State 
Government. The State Electricity Regulatory Commission, in its tariff order of 
16th March, 2003, had given various tariffs for various categories of 
consumers. Simultaneously, the State Government had announced a scheme 
of direct subsidy to small and marginal farmers and to

expenditure. Therefore, the mention of 'non-Plan expenditure' is not at all 
indicating mere non-Plan expenditure like interest and mere subsidies. But it 
includes other areas also. Therefore, th e confusion also prevails. When it is 
so, we have to reach some targets. Reaching targets means, development 
and inflation. If you take the Fifth Five Year Plan, the Sixth Five Year Plan, the

the fiscal deficit. I agree that fiscal defi cit should be within  some limit. There

per cent. It is a new phenomenon. Then, I talk about the percentage of GDP.

severely affected. Sir, unless greater  emphasis is given on the agriculture

confronting the country now is the de volution of powers to the States. 
Keep the very vital department alone. What is the purpose of running a 
Rural Development Department in Delhi and chalking out all the Centrally- 
sponsored schemes, wasting all the money - at least, 86 paise out of a 
rupee? You are wasting the manpower ; you are wasting the money, you 
are wasting the financial set-up of our country. Demolish it. Why is there a 
Social Welfare Department in Delhi? Wh at is the purpose? Just to promote 
some NGOs and associations like that. All the powers have to be devolved 
to the States and to the Panchayati Raj so that a very good Government at 
the Centre can be run with the vital Departments alone. To    fight    the 
terrorists and to integrate our country, de centralisation of powers is very 
necessary. I am very sorry, the major parties are not at all worried about the 
situation. Otherwise, the Sarkaria  Commission Report would not have 
remained in the almirah for so many years. Unless you realise this, you can't 
achieve the targets in your dream.  That is the crucial thing. 
Another point is the basic economic reforms. You are privatising very 
important public sector units. You ar e inviting foreign companies to the 
country and giving them powers. I am not against foreign investment in 
spheres where it helps our country and where it is necessary. But what is 
going on? Chapter-IV of our Constitution St ates clearly that concentration of 
wealth and concentration of means of production should not be allowed. The 
monopoly houses should not be permitted to do that. Now, what is 
happening? The wealth is being concentrated. It is not being distributed fairly 
among the people. You can calculat e the GDP. You can calculate the 
development figures. But whom does it go? The wealth goes to the wealthy 
people again and again. The statistics sh ow that for the last 10-12 years the 
gap between the rich and the poor has widened. You can see it with your 
naked eyes. The wealth is being c oncentrated. The corporate houses,

family group,  declares Rs.50,000 crores and another declares

SHRI SURENDRA LATH (Orissa): Madam, thank you very much for 
giving me the opportunity to participate in this important debate on the 
financial health of the States. This is  a very important matter. The rapid 
deterioration in the condition of the State finances is an issue of serious 
concern. The devastating financial cond ition has been an important constraint 
in creating quality infrastructure and development and reduces the investment 
in social sectors. 
Madam, the gross fiscal deficit of t he States is increasing every year. 
The total gross fiscal deficit of the States in 2001-02 rose to Rs. 1,06,595 
crores, which is 4.3 per cent of the GD P. This is because of a decrease in 
revenue receipts and an increase in reve nue expenditure. The States have to 
resort to a high level of borrowings to meet the increased revenue 
expenditure. This causes increase in large scale fiscal revenue deficit. The 
high magnitude of interest payment pr e-empts revenue receipts, thereby put 
constraints on developmental activities of the States. 
Madam, there are various reasons for this state of affairs. A very 
significant reason is the enormous increase in the wage bills and pension 
liabilities. After the implementation of  the recommendations of the Fifth Pay 
Commission, the wage bills of the Stat es increased to a great extent. The 
share of revenue deficit increased from 38 per cent in 1997-98, to 60 per cent, 
in 1998-99 due to the pay revision. T he pension liabilities of the States have 
also shown a sharp rise, and it also enhanced the revenue expenditure to a 
large extent. The fiscal deficit which was 3 per cent of the GDP, in 1997-
98,.increased sharply to 4.2 per cent, in 1998-99 and 4.6 per cent in 
1999-2000. 
288 

[5 August, 2003] RAJYA SABHA 
Secondly, Madam, the State Gove rnments have also invested large 
sums in public sector undertakings, but t he receipts from these public sector 
undertakings in the form of dividend and pr ofit is negligible. Most of the State 
public sector undertakings are making huge losses and need budgetary 
support, which causes an additional burden on the State finances. Most of the 
State Electricity Boards were making huge losses due to a large amount of 
subsidy given by some States. 
Madam, the other reason for financial indiscipline is that the 
outstanding guarantees issued by the State Governments have risen in the 
recent years. There is an additional burden on the State finances due to a 
default by the entities for whom t he guarantees have been issued. The non-
adherence to the payment obligation committed by the States in respect of the 
guarantee already provided by them has adverse implications on the 
sovereign credibility, and, thus, may create problems in future, in raising 
resources from the market. Because of these reasons, many States have put 
a ceiling on issuing guarantees in order to restrict the increase in the debt 
burden of the States. 
Madam, because of the financial constraints and the increase in 
revenue expenditure and spending on unproductive expenditure, there is little 
left for making a provision for expenditure for development and other social 
services. There is a decline in the Pl an expenditure on health, education,

Reduction in holidays 
*241.   SHRI LALITBHAI MEHTA: † 
 SHRIMATI SAVITA SHARDA: 
Will the Minister of PERSONNEL, PUBLIC GRIEVANCS AND 
PENSIONS be pleased to state: 
(a) the number of days a year, the Government of India employees work 
considering holidays of Saturdays, Su ndays, Gazetted Holidays, Restricted 
Holidays and various types of leave availed by them; 
(b) whether Government have examined the possibility of reducing the 
Gazetted Holidays by permitting employ ees of respective religious faiths a 
holiday on that particular day and avoid closing of Government offices; 
(c) whether Government have also examined the possibility of restoring a six day 
week to increase the number of working days; and 
(d) whether Government propose to conduct any study on the effects of 
observance of so many holidays on developmental works and routine 
administration of Government of India? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF PERSONNEL, 
PUBLIC GRIEVANCES AND PENSIONS (SHRI HARIN PATHAK): (a) to (d) 
A Statement is laid on the Table of the House. 
† The question was actually asked on the floor of the House by Shri Lalitbhai Mehtra. 

RAJYA  SABHA [6 August, 2003] 
Statement 
(a) So far as Central Government Administrative Offices covered by 
the Five day week system are con cerned, employees avail themselves 
of Saturdays and Sundays (about 104 in a year), two Restricted Holidays 
and 17 Gazetted Holidays (out of which normally 3-4 holidays fall on 
Saturdays and Sundays, thereby reduc ing the effective holidays to an 
average of 14 per year). 
Those Central Government employees who are governed by the Central Civil 
Services (Leave) Rules, 1972 are entitled to 30 days Earned Leave, 20 days Half Pay 
Leave and 8 days Casual Leave (for admini strative offices) per year.These are, 
however, personal to the employees and are availed by them as per their 
requirement, subject to sanction of  the leave, based on administrative 
exigencies. Earned Leave if not availed during the year may be carried forward 
subject to a ceiling of 300 days, Half Pay Leave if not availed during the year 
may be carried forward without any limit. Casual Leave and Restricted Holidays 
cannot, however, be carried forward if not availed within the Calendar year. 
Therefore, the number of days in a year the Government of India employees work 
vary depending upon the number of days of leave availed by him/her during the 
year. The maximum number of days Central Government administrative offices 
remain open in a year is about 247 days. 
Other than the Central Government offices functioning on five day week 
basis a large number of Central Government organisations, including Industrial and 
Operational Organisations function on six day week basis keeping in view their 
operational requirements. In fact some organisations related with delivery of 
essential services, work round the clock. Therefore, the number of days 
Government employees work in these units, in a year, is essentially dependent on 
the nature of functions being performed by these units, and the regulations 
governing the hours of work and leave in those units. 
(b) It is not desirable to restrict employees to avail themselves holidays based 
on religious faiths only.

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF RURAL 
DEVELOPMENT (SHRI ANNASAHEB M.K. PATIL): (a) to (c) A statement is 
laid on the Table of the House. 
Statement 
(a) Under the Indira Awaas Yojana (IAY), some of the States/UTs are not 
sending Monthly Progress Reports regularly. 
(b) The Central assistance under the scheme is released every year to the 
District Rural Development Agencies (DRDAs) in two instalments, subject to 
the fulfillment of the following conditions. 
(i) The first instalment amounting to 50% of the Central allocation for a 
particular DRDA is released in the beginning of the financial year, if 
second instalment during the previous year was claimed and released 
without any condition. 
(ii) The second instalment of funds for the district is released on receipt of 
request from the DRDAs in the pres cribed proforma alongwith Audit 
Report/UC of previous year etc. after utilising 60% of total available 
funds including opening balance and State share etc. 
(iii) Central share to the tune of 3/4 times of the amount exceeding 
permissible opening balance in the district (i.e. 15% of the district 
allocation of the previous year) is deducted from the amount of 
second instalment. 
(iv) The graded cut from 10% to 30% of Central allocation is imposed on 
the quantum of second instalment if complete proposal is received late 
(from January to March of the financial year). 
All this is to ensure that the funds allotted to the States under the Scheme 
are being utilised and are not being reappropriated for other purposes. 
(c) State-wise details of amount allocated, released and utilised under the 
Indira Awaas Yojana (IAY) during 2002-03 are annexed as Statement-I.

*249. SHRI MURLI DEORA: Will the Minister of HOME AFFAIRS be 
pleased to state: 
(a) whether NDMC suffers staggering loss of Rs. 3.84 crore annually; 
(b) if so, the reasons therefor; 
(c) whether abnormal delay in revi sion of licence fee, improper 
maintenance of records and vital information has become the practice there; 
(d) if so, the reasons therefor; and 
(e) the steps taken to remedy the situation?

(SHRI HARIN PATHAK): (a) to (e) A statement is laid on the Table of the 
House. 
Statement 
(a) and (b) The Chief Auditor of New Delhi Municipal Council in her 
Audit Report for the year ended March, 2000 had, inter alia, pointed out that 
the Council had in respect of 569 stalls transferred from the Enforcement 
Department to the Estate Department sustained a loss of 
30

Rs. 3.84 crore on account of non-implementation of the two Resolutions passed 
in September, 1979 and March, 1986 in the matter of revision of license fee. 
The New Delhi Municipal Council have reported that these observations are 
under examination. 
(c) to (e) There has been some delay in revision of license fee and lack of 
proper maintenance of records. However, the Council have initiated action to 
computerize the records relating to de mand and collection of license fee in 
order to streamline the system.

System to forewarn people about cyclones 
*259.   MS. PRAMILA BOHIDAR: 
SHRI B.J. PANDA: 
Will the Minister of HOME AFFAIRS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government are aware that  in the last cyclone there was 
heavy loss of life and property as the residents of the coastal areas could not 
be forewarned well before time; 
(b) if so, whether Government have now developed any system to 
forewarn the people before such a natural calamity takes on them; and 
(c) if so, the success of such a system and how far it has been used to 
save the lives and property of coastal people? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HOME AFFAIRS 
(SHRI SWAMI CHINMAYANAND): (a) In the Orissa Super-Cyclone of 
1999, there was heavy loss of life and property not on account of a lack of 
forewarning but due to the intensity of the cyclone, heavy storm surge and 
continuous down pour. 
(b) and (c) The cyclonic systems both in the Bay of Bengal and the 
Arabian Sea are being monitored and tracked by the India Meteorological 
Department (IMD) through a chain of high power coastal radars, high wind speed 
recorders and a network of surface and upper air observatories 
51 

RAJYA  SABHA [6 August, 2003] 
along the coastline. India's present capability is such that no cyclone 
approaching the Indian coast can escape detection and the information is made 
available through the INSAT based Cyclonic Warning Dissemination Systems and 
radio and TV channels both at the national and regional levels. The technology 
upgradation of the monitoring systems is also a continuing process at the 
IMD.The cyclone tracking and warning systems have proved to be effective. 
Cyclone alerts and warnings are bein g communicated to the States well in 
time.

Steps to boost FDI in coal and mining sector 
1805. SHRl R.S. GAVAI: Will the Minister of COAL be pleased to 
state: 
(a) whether Government have formulated any stragegy to boost the 
Foreign Direct Investment in coal and mining sector; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; 
(c) whether Government are considering to set up a Regulatory Authority 
for the country's coal sector; 
(d) if so, the details thereof; and 
(e) if not, the reasons therefor? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF COAL (SHRl 
PRAHLAD SINGH PATEL): (a) and (b) In order to attract Foreign 
67 

RAJYA SABHA [6 August, 2003] 
Direct Investment in coal sector the Government have decided that the private 
Indian companies setting up or operating power projects as well as coal or 
lignite mines for captive consumption in such projects may be allowed foreign 
equity upto 100% provided that the coal or lignite produced by them is meant 
entirely for captive consumption in power generation. 
100% foreign investment in the equity of an Indian subsidiary of a 
foreign company or in the equity of an Indian company for setting up of coal 
processing plants in India may be allowed subject to the conditions that such an 
Indian subsidiary or the Indian company (a) shall not do coal mining and (b) 
shall not sell the washed coal or sized coal from their Coal Processing Plants 
in the open market and shall supply the washed coal or sized coal from their 
Coal Processing Plants to the respective parties sending raw coal to such Coal 
Processing Plants for washing or sizing. 
The other private Indian companies engaged in exploration or mining of 
coal and lignite for captive consumption for production of iron and steel and 
production of cement may be allowed foreign equity upto 74%. 
The Government has liberalized its Foreign Direct Investment (FDI) policy 
in the mining sector which allows foreign equity holding upto 100%, on the 
automatic route for all non-fuel and non-atomic minerals except diamonds 
and precious stones, This covers exploration, mining, mineral processing and 
metallurgy. In the case of diamonds and precious stones, foreign equity upto 74% 
is allowed on the automatic route for both exploration and mining operations. 
However, proposals seeking higher than 74% foreign equity for diamonds & 
precious stones are considered by the Foreign Investment Promotion Board 
(FIPB).The Mines & Minerals (Development & Regulation) Act, 1957 has also 
been suitably amended to make it more investor friendly. 
(c) and (d) Keeping in view the recommendations of the Committee on 
Integrated Coal Policy (Chari Committee), the Central Government decided in 
February, 1997, among other things, to set up an Independent Body to perform the 
functions of monitoring and processing the proposals for exploration of coal and 
lignite in the country and allotment of new coal and lignite blocks to Indian 
Companies, in public and private sector, on the basis of competitive bidding. 
Proposal was conceived in the context of the amendment to the Coal Mines 
(Nationalisation) Act, 1973 to allow 
68 

 
[6 August, 2003] RAJYA SABHA 
non-captive coal mining by the private sector. Necessary action in the matter 
may be taken after the Coal Mines (Nationalisation) Bill, 2000 is enacted by 
the Parliament. 
(e) Question does not arise.

Details of Welfare Measures for Defence Personnel and their Families 
Medical 
There is a good network of hospitals for the serving personnel. All 
military hospitals attend to day to day medical requirements of servicemen and 
their families. 
Specialized Medical Treatment 
(a) Research and Referral Hospital: For serving soldiers requiring 
specialized medical treatment, a supe r specialist hospital is available 
at New Delhi. 
(b) Paraplegis Rehabilitation Centres (PRCS)-.Two PRCs, At Kirkee and 
Mohali are available for rehabilitation of disabled soldiers. 
(c) St. Dunstan's After Care Organisation: This organisation provides 
training to the visually handicapped servicemen at the national 
Institute for visually handicapped at Dehradun. 
(d) Artificial Limb Centre (ALC): One ALC is available at Pune for 
providing of artificial limbs to disabled soldiers. 
2. Now, a medical scheme called Ex-servicemen Contributory Health 
Scheme (ECHS) has been approved, which caters for comprehensive medical 
cover to the ex-servicemen in receipt  of any kind of pension including 
disability pension and family pensioners, spouse as also 
80 

[6 August, 2003] RAJYA SABHA 
legitimate children and wholly dependent parents.The scheme envisages to 
establish 104 augmented medical inspection rooms at military stations and 123 
new poly clinics at non military stations.The scheme contributory in nature has 
commenced w.e.f. 1st April 2003 and would be fully implemented by March 
2008. 
3. For the time being till ECHS becomes operational, service hospitals 
would continue with entitled treatment and AGI's extended Medical Benefit 
Scheme (MBS) and financial assistance for AG's Welfare Fund and KSB 
for medical treatment would also continue. 
Financial Assistance 
4. Financial assistance is granted to the ex-servicemen, widows and 
their dependent family members from Raksha Mantri's Discretionary Fund 
(RMDF) and AG's Welfare Fund for assistance to old, infirm, for marriage 
of daughters, repair of houses, medical treatment etc. 
Education 
5. In order to provide quality education to the children of army personnel 
posted deployed in far flung areas, 116 army schools have been 
established. Besides, the Air Force have established 148 schools in most 
of the units to provide educational facilities to the children of air force 
personnel and the Navy has establishe d 9 Naval Public Schools. 7 schools 
have been established by Air Force Wives Welfare Association for mentally 
and physically challenged children. 
Educational concessions 
6. Children of defence personnel killed or permanently disabled in action 
who are studying in institutions under the department of Education are granted 
complete exemption from tuition fee and other fee levied by the institution. 
7. Educational scholarships are awarded by the Army, the Navy and the Air 
Force to the wards of serving soldiers, based on both merit and means. 
8. 28 seats in MBBS, 1 seat in BDS, 2 seats in Engineering in 
Annamalai University and 2 seats each in the 7 IITs (subject to qualifying 
81 

RAJYA SABHA [6 August, 2003] 
the Joint Entrance Examination) are available for the wards of servicemen and ex-
servicemen. 
Vocational Training 
9. The three service Headquarters make arrangement for Vocational 
Training to their respective servicemen at various civil institutions, prior to 
their retirement, for their post retirement settlement. 
Housing 
10. Army Welfare Housing Organisation provides limited no. of houses to 
servicemen and ex-servicemen in select stations at reasonable costs. Similar 
housing facilities are provided by Air Force Naval Housing Board to Air Force 
and Naval personnel. 
11. Various State Governments have made reservations for serving/ retired 
defence personnel/dependents in allotment of house sites/houses. 
12. 37 War Memorial Hostels have been constructed to provide 
accommodation to wards of war bereaved and disabled personnel to enable 
them to pursue their studies. 
Transit Facilities 
13. Over 252 Sainik Aram Grahs have been established at many stations 
where servicemen have to transit while being on duty or proceeding to/returning 
from leave. Besides, 15 holiday homes have also been established at select 
stations. 
14. Journey by air is provided to serv icemen and their families while 
travelling on duty or leave to and from Leh sector in J&K. 
15.75% concession in rail fare and airfare in Indian Airlines domestic flights 
is provided to recipients of certain gallantry award winners and to widows of 
posthumous winners of the gallantry awards along with a companion. 
Canteen Facilities 
16. Items of daily needs are provided at concessional rates to servicemen 
and their families through the Canteen Stores Department and the Unit Run 
Canteens.

and suggested for amending Indian Penal Code with a view to provide justice 
to the women victims of violence and to deal with their multifacet problems; 
(b) if so, whether keeping in view increasing incidents of atrocities 
against women, Government are contemplating to make necessary 
amendments in this regard; and 
(c) if so, the details thereof and if not, the reasons therefor? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HOME AFFAIRS 
(SHRI I.D. SWAMI): (a) The Chairman of the erstwhile Committee on 
Criminal Justice Reforms participat ed in the seminar organized by the 
National Commission for women on "Women Victims of Crime and 
Violence" on 31st May, 2003 in his personal capacity as the Committee had 
become functus officio after submission of the report on April 21, 2003. The 
Commission has informed that he referred, to the need for reforms and 
revamping criminal justice system. 
(b) and (c) The Law Commission in its 172nd Report prepared after  
†Original notice of the question was received in Hindi. 
108 

[6 August, 2003] RAJYA SABHA 
taking into consideration suggestions from various women' organizations has 
recommended changes for widening scope of the offence in section 375 of the 
Indian Penal Code, 1860 and to make it gender neutral. Other changes 
recommended include amendment to section 376 and 376A to 376D, insertion of 
a new section 376E dealing with unlawful sexual contact with young persons 
below the age of sixteen years, deleti on of section 377 and enhancement of 
punishment in section 509 of Indian Penal Code, 1860. Various consequential 
changes in the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 and the Indian Evidence Act, 
1872 have also been recommended. 
The 172nd Report of the Law Commission has been referred to State 
Governments and Union Territory Administration for their views as the

CONVENTIONAL ENERGY SOURCES (SHRI M. KANNAPPAN): (a) and

Renewable Energy Development Agency (IREDA). The Planning

Ranganadi Hydro Electric Dam 
1879. DR. ARUN KUMAR SARMA: Will the Minister of POWER be 
pleased to state: 
(a) whether discharge of water from Ranganadi Hydro Electric Dam 
through Dikrong River of Assam has taken place; and 
(b) if so, the details thereof and the ac tion contemplated to take up flood 
protection measures of Dikrong River as part of the total project? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF POWER 
(SHRIMATI JAYAWANTI MEHTA): (a) Yes, Sir.The transfer of water from 
Ranganadi Hydro Electric Project to th e Dikrong River has taken place since 
the commissioning of Ranganadi H.E. Project in January, 2002. 
(b) The water conductor system of the project has been designed for a peak 
discharge of 160 cumecs.The actual discharge, into Dikrong River, however, 
depends on the generation at Ranganadi Power House. In lean season, only 1 unit 
of the project can be run at 65 MW continuously which would discharge about 26 
cumes of water to Dikrong River. 
Due to additional maximum discharge of 160 cumecs in monsoon 
months, rise of water level in different stretches of the Dikrong River in Assam 
portion would range from 7cm. to 12 cm. At Banderdewa, the rise would be 7 
cm. and at Sissapathar the same will be 12 cm. The observed peak flow of 
Dikrong River at Sissapathar bridge is 2500 cumes (upto 1997). The 
incremental discharge of 160 cumecs is very insignificant in comparison. 
The flood protection work of the downstream reaches of Dikrong river 
beyond Banderdewa Bridge as existing (without transfer of 160 cumecs of 
water from Ranganadi basin to Dikrong basin) is not sufficient to retain the 
observed 2500 cumecs discharge of river Dikrong during the peak flood 
season. No embankment has so far been constructed by the 
134 

[6 August, 2003] RAJYA SABHA 
State   Government to cater to observed 2500 cumecs of discharge peak flood 
to protect the population. 
Keeping this in view, NEEPCO has decided to keep the power house 
under shutdown during such peak floods  and no additional water would be 
discharged to Dikrong River during flood season.

National Housing Policy 
1889. SHRI K. RAHMAN KHAN: Will the Minister of RURAL 
DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state: 
(a) whether the objective of the national housing policy to end 
shelterlessness by the Ninth Plan ha s been achieved; if so, the details 
thereof; 
(b) the number of housing units built up so far against the target fixed for 
the purpose; 
(c) what are the hurdles experienced in achieving the targets; and 
(d) what steps are being contemplated for successful implementation of 
National Housing Corporation? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF RURAL 
DEVELOPMENT (SHRI ANNASAHEB M. K. PATIL): (a) to (d) The Central 
Government announced in 1998 a National Housing and Habitat Policy which 
aims at providing 'Housing for AH'. Pursuant to the National Housing Policy, 
special Action Plan was prepared for construction of additional 13 lakh new 
houses annually in the rural areas in addition to the existing target of about 
12.50 lakh houses annually with an emphasis on extending benefits to the poor 
and the deprived. During the last three years of the 9th Five Plan period, against 
the target of 75.90 lakh, around 52.38 lakh houses have been constructed under 
the Indira Awaas Yojana (IAY) and thr ough HUDCO & National Housing 
Bank (NHB). One of the major constraints in implementation of the Action 
Plan is inadequate budgetary resources. As a result, shelterlessness in rural 
areas by the end of 9th Plan could not be achieved in full.

On the implementation of Conditional Access System and criteria for 
uplinking for foreign channels 
Ǜी संजय िनरुपम (महाराÍटर्): महोदय, मȅ आपके  माध्यम से सूचना और Ģसारण मंतर्ी का 
ध्यान कं डीशनल एक्सेस िसÎटम को लागू करने का फै सला और अपिंलिंकग के  िलए फॉरेन चैनल का 
जा कर्ाइटेिरया है, उसकी ओर आकिर्षत करता हूं। 
THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE MINISTRY OF INFORMATION 
AND BROADCASTING (SHRI RAVI SHANKAR PRASAD): Hon'ble 
Chairperson, Shri Sanjay Nirupam and other Members have drawn my 
attention to the implementation of Conditional Access System (CAS), and also 
the criteria for uplinking policy for foreign channels. Let me inform this hon'ble 
House about the decisions taken by the Government. I would like to make a 
brief statement on the issues raised by the hon. Members in their notices. 
The genesis of this exercise lies in  the fact that having mandated the 
Conditional Access System through an amendment in the Cable Television 
Networks (Regulation) Act, 1995, and the prevalent confusion and chaos and 
uncertainties regarding rates and lack of  transparency in the system, it was 
necessary that the consumers be protec ted from this arbitrariness and a 
scientific rational approach be adopted for working out the rates of free-to-air 
channels in the basic service tier. 
As the hon. Members are aware, t he Government had set up a 'Task 
Force' comprising the various stakeholders like Cable Operators' Association,    
Multi-System   Operators   (MSOs),   Broadcasters,   Consumer 
180 

[6 August, 2003] RAJYA SABHA 
Electronics and T.V. Manufacturers ' Association (CETMA) besides the 
Consumer Groups and Technical Expert s to examine the various issues 
related to and oversee the implementation of the Conditional Access System 
(CAS) as provided under the Cable Television Networks (Regulation) Act, 
1995. 
The Cost Accounts Branch (CAB) of the Ministry of Finance was also 
requested to commission a study and the effort was to get a feedback from 
the cable operators on important issues. Several meetings were also held 
where they were invited to give their suggestions/comments. The C.A.B. .had 
detailed discussions with the technical experts, including equipment 
manufacturers, Broadcast Engineering Consultants India Ltd. (BECIL), etc. 
Pursuant to the recommendations  of this Task Force, the 
Government, through a notification issued on 14 th January, 2003, notified the 
introduction of C.A.S. with effect from 15 th July, 2003, in the four metros., and 
through a notification issued on 7 th May specified the minimum number of 
free-to-air channels to be included in the package of channels forming the 
basic service tier to be Rs.30 and the maximum amount which a cable 
operator can demand from a subscriber to  be Rs.72. I may also point out that 
the few Multi System Operators have alre ady assured that they will be able to 
show between 60 to 70 free-to-air channels within the maximum cost of 
Rs.72/-. 
I. FOLLOW-UP ACTION BY THE MINISTRY 
I would like to assure the" hon. members that there has been no 
confusion in the implement ation of C.A.S. On the contrary, the Government 
has taken a number of initiatives for its smooth implementat ion in the four 
metres. I would like to inform the House that the Government has been in 
constant and continuous dialogue with the representatives of stakeholders in 
the industry, i.e. manufacturers, broadcasters, MSOs and cable operators. 
The present state of pr eparedness indicated that adequate Set Top Boxes 
were not likely to be available by the deadline, i.e., 15th July, 2003. Hence, 
the Government has deferred the im plementation of the CAS to 1st 
September, 2003 and proposes to im plement it in a phased zone-wise 
manner in the three metres of Delhi, Kolkata and Mumbai. As far as possible, 
these zones have been carved out with distinctive features in order 
181 

RAJYA SABHA [6 August, 2003] 
to provide minimum overlap of the services between zones of each city. As far 
as Chennai is concerned, based on the feed-back from the MSOs in Chennai, 
it has been decided to implement it at one go. 
The intervening period will be used to step up preparedness, build 
up consumer awareness and enable the im portation/manufacture of boxes in 
greater volumes. 
The Ministry of Finance has also reduced the customs duty from 
50.8 per cent to 5 per cent which ha s been extended until 30th September, 
2003 through its Notification dated 29th  July, 2003. It has been estimated that 
analogue Set Top Boxes would cost about Rs. 2,500/- and digital Set Top 
Boxes would cost between Rs. 2,700/- and Rs. 3,000/-. A few MSOs have also 
offered attractive introductory offers and easy affordable schemes through hire 
purchase, loan schemes, instalment basis, refundable deposit with a nominal 
daily rental, etc. As on 31.7.2003, 1,07,882 Set Top Boxes have been 
imported -- this is on the basis of the information given by the Customs 
Department. It is also expected t hat with the increasing demand and 
indigenous production and supply, the prices are likely to fall further. Steps are 
also being taken to ensure quality of the Set Top Boxes through random 
sample testing of the boxes of different  manufacturers. Visits are being made 
to head-ends to assess the level of upgradation and preparedness. All this is 
aimed at making it consumer-friendly. 
Now,  I would like to discuss the criteria on uplinking policy for foreign 
channels. 
II. UPLINKING POLICY 
The uplinking policy has been gradually developing over a span of 
five years. 
(i) In June 1998, the Cabinet, fo r the first time, permitted Indian 
satellite channels (with Indian equity not less than 80 per cent 
and effective management control in the hands of resident 
Indians) to uplink from India through VSNL only. 
182 

[6 August, 2003) RAJYA SABHA 
(ii) In March 1999, the Cabinet permitted all Indian companies (who 
were broadcasters and were as defined above) to uplink from 
India without being mandated to go through VSNL only. 
(iii)   In July 2000, the Cabinet approved the following: 
(a) Setting up of hubs/teleports by companies incorporated in 
India with not more than 49 per  cent foreigrt equity holding, 
including from NRI, OCB and PIO. 
(b) Unlinking of all TV channels irrespective of ownership, 
equity structure or management  control, which aimed at 
Indian viewer ship. 
(c) Uplinking to Indian News Agencies accredited with PIB and 
whose 100 per cent ownership and management control 
was with Indians. 
(iv) In the year 2002, there was a fe lt need that in influencing public 
opinion, television is, if not more, at least, as powerful as the 
print media. The views obtained in the first report of the Press 
Commission, on the subject of foreign nationals as owners of 
newspapers and periodicals, had continuing relevance for the 
Broadcasting sector also. The Co mmission had observed that it 
would be highly desirable that proprietorial interest in 
newspapers should vest predominantly in Indian hands. 
Taking note of such concerns, a note was taken to Cabinet in March, 
2003 for considering "imposition of  restrictions on ownership and 
management control of TV channels, telecasting news and current affairs 
programmes, as it was felt that these concerns had not been adequately 
addressed in the existing policy on uplinking of TV channels from India. The 
arguments given in favour of restrict ions were that a foreign owned and 
controlled TV news channel may exercise an unhealthy influence on our 
democratic processes to suit vested foreign interests and may pose a threat 
to our social and cultural value systems. 
183 

RAJYA SABHA (6 August, 2003] 
While the last concern was equally applicable to all the foreign 
content telecasting channels, other concer ns were valid largely in respect of 
News and Current Affairs channels only. The potential for mischief against 
safety and security of the State was acknowledged to be more with a channel 
which is largely dedicated to News and Current Affairs' programmes than with 
other channels. 
The Cabinet vide its decision of I8 th March, 2003 inter alia approved 
foreign ownership/management control restrictions to be placed on channels 
having any element of News and Current Affairs' content and allowed to uplink 
from India. The guidelines, issued on 26th March, 2003, laid down the 
following eligibility criteria for a company uplinking News and Current Affairs 
channels including, inter alia, the following : 
(a) To be registered/incorporated in India under the Companies Act, 
1956. 
(b) Foreign equity holding in the applicant company not to exceed 
26 per cent of the total paid up capital. 
(c) Majority of its Board of Directors to be Resident Indians. 
(d) CEO of the applicant company, known by any designation, 
and/or Head of the channel to be Resident India. 
(e) News Editor (s) or authority(ies) exercising editorial control over 
news and current affairs programme(s) of the channel(s) to be 
Resident Indians. 
Throughout the evolution of the upli nking policy in stages, ownership 
and management control to vest in Indian hands has remained a prime 
concern. This was sought to be addr essed categorically in March, 2003, 
particularly, in relation to News and Current Affairs' channels. Further, by an 
order of July 15, 2003, an inter-Ministerial Group has been set up to examine 
the foreign exchange norms/guidelines, particularly, relating to uplinking of 
news and current affairs channels. The case of one of the application seeking 
uplinking as per extant guidelines is under examination.

rise has been only three times.   That is

Commission, which is now functioning as  a non-statutory advisory body, on 
the basis of Government Resolutions of 4th April 1999, as amended further on 
13th August, 2002. 
The Commission is envisaged to be a multi-member body, consisting 
of a Central Vigilance Commissioner as Chairperson, and not more than two 
Vigilance Commissioners as Members, to be appointed by the President by 
warrant under his hand and seal, after recommendations for their appointment 
are made by a committee consisting of the hon. Prime Minister as the 
Chairperson, the Minister of Home Affa irs and the Leader of the Opposition in 
the House of People as Members. The Commission will exercise 
superintendence over vigilance administrat ion. But, this power is restricted in 
a manner that the superintendence is not inconsistent with the directions 
issued by the Central Government, mainly, because it is the Central 
Government, which is accountable to the Parliament. The area of preventive 
vigilance includes Government rules and procedures that are internal to the / 
administration in the Government and where the Central Government should 
continue to exercise its Executive control. 
Madam, in the meantime, the work re lating to the Central Bureau of 
Investigation has been transferred to  the Cabinet Secretariat from the 
Department of Personnel and Training . Secondly, the appointments at the 
level of Superintendent of Police and above are proposed to be brought within 
the purview of the CBI Selection Committee in the light of the directions of the 
Supreme Court in Vineet Narain's case. Accordingly, two official amendments 
in regard to Clause 26 of the Central Vigilance Commission Bill, 2003, as 
passed by the Lok Sabha, are also proposed to be moved.

Unemployment problem 
*268.  SHRI RAJEEV SHUKLA: †† 
SHRI RAJKUMAR DHOOT: 
Will the Minister of LABOUR be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that the avenues for employment are shrinking and the 
number of unemployed and semi-employed persons are soaring over the years; 
(b) the generation of employment opportunities planned in different 
categories during the period 2003-04 and 2004-05; 
(c) what has been and what is likely to be the impact of cut in jobs in 
Government PSUs, divestment in PSUs and closure of industrial units in creating 
new job opportunities; and 
(d) whether Government have set any target to provide employment to 
every eligible citizen of the country? 
THE MINISTER OF LABOUR (SHRI SAHIB SINGH VERMA): (a) to (d) A 
Statement is laid on the Table of the House. 
Statement 
(a to d) Estimates of employment and unemployment are obtained through 
quinquennial labour force surveys conducted by National Sample Survey 
Organisation. Last such survey was conducted during 1999-2000. As per 
these surveys, estimated employment in  the country on usual status basis has 
gone up from approximately 374 million in 1993-94 to 397 million on 1999-2000. 
Number of unemployed during 1993-94 and 1999-2000 was approximately 75 
lakh and 90 lakh respectively. 
The Special Group headed by Dr. S.  P. Gupta, Member, Planning 
Commission has recommended strategy and programmes which have been 
considered while formulating the 10th Plan, for targeting creation of 50 million 
employment opportunities (10 million per year) during the 10th Plan period 
(2002-2007). It identified the activities where there is a major potential of large 
new job opportunities as in agricultur e, including social forestry, animal 
husbandry, fishing, horticulture and related areas and small and medium 
industries, construction, tourism, information

that with the target of achieving 10 millio n jobs per year, it will be possible to

Organised sector constitutes about 7%  of the total employment in the 
country. Loss of jobs, if any, in Public Sector Undertakings (PSUs), disinvested 
PSUs and industrial units, may not have any significant effect on total 
employment in the country.

2. As on 30th June, 2003, the stocks of sugar in Maharashtra and Uttar 
Pradesh were 54.52 lakh tonnes and 31.27 lakh tonnes respectively, as against

date of the previous season.

monthly "regulated release" mechanism and through exports to promote which 
the Central Government have, inter-alia, taken the following steps:- 
(i) Quantitative restrictions on export of sugar have been lifted; 
(ii) Factories exporting sugar have be en allowed exemption from levy on 
the quantity of sugar exported;

made at the end of 18 months from the date of export;

allowed to claim reimbursement of expenditure incurred on internal 
transport and freight charges on export shipments of sugar; 
(vi) With effect from 14th February, 2003, the sugar factories have been 
allowed neutralization of oc ean freight disadvantage on export 
shipments of sugar @Rs. 350 per tonne. 
4. The Essential Commodities Act, 1955 has recently been amended 
vide Notification dated 2nd June, 2003 to provide for effective 
implementation of "regulated release" mechanism.

Some of the important findings of C and AG 
55. Quality of services of Mahanagar Telephone Nigam Limited. 
55.1 Summary of important findings and Highlights; 
MTNL has been providing various basic and value added services to 
subscribers through its networks in Delhi and Mumbai. In a majority of cases 
there have been abnormal delays vis-a-vis norms prescribed in providing 
services to subscribers, which led to dissatisfaction and inconvenience to them. 
Delays were specially long in the case of shifting of telephones, telephone transfer 
to another person's name and clearance of telephone faults. MTNL has not even 
fixed norms/targets for providing certain services. Even its comparative 
performance in providing services to different areas of Delhi varied considerably: 
the best quality of service was provided to Central Area, while the East Area 
received the worst. In a majority of cases the quality of services was poor on 
account of insufficient coordination. The overall quality of various services 
provided by MTNL, remained below average. 
Some of the important findings are highlighted below: 
 In case of Mumbai unit, the percent age of execution of OBs within the 
prescribed norm of 15 days increased from 52 per cent in 1998-99 to 
64 per cent in 1999-2000 but thereafter declined to 50 per

execution of OBs within the 15 days norm increased from 13 per cent 
in 1998-99 to 31 per cent in 2000-01; it was 30 per cent in 2001-02. 
(Paragraph 55.5) 
 In shifting of telephone connections the performance of Delhi and 
Mumbai units of MTNL was very unsatisfactory as only 24 per cent 
OBs (Delhi unit) in case of 'other area shifting' and nine per cent 
(Delhi Unit) and 13 per cent (Mum bai Unit) OBs in case of 'local 
Shifting' were completed within the prescribed norm. Besides, in case

(Paragraph ,55.8) 
 Time taken in execution of majority of OBs for transfer of telephone

relations (83 per cent OBs) ranged from six days to six months. 
(Paragraph 55.7) 
 There were delays in transfer of telephone connections to a third 
party. There were no time norms and in over 80 per cent of the cases 
of issue of demand notes for payment of transfer fee and in execution 
of OBs; from the date of their issue,  time taken ranged from six days 
to six months. 
(Paragraph 55.8) 
 Time taken for execution of 46 per cent OBs for restoration of

†1940. SHRI LAJPAT RAI: 
SHRI RAJIV RANJAN SINGH 'LALAN': 
Will the Minister of COMMUNICATIONS AND INFORMATION

(a) whether it is a fact that the expenditure on the Information Technology

(b) if not, assessment of Government in this regard; 
(c) whether it is also a fact that E-governance started in India five years 
back; and 
(d) if so, the names of the Stat es where the compliance of the E-
governance policy has begun? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF COMMUNICATIONS 
AND INFORMATION TECHNOLOGY (SHRI SU. THIRUNAVUKKARASAR): 
(a) No, Sir. 
(b) According to NASSCOM estimates, India currently spends about 1.1 per 
cent of its GDP on Information Technology. This works out to about Rs. 22, 
757 crore in the year 2001-02, or about US $ 4.8 billion. 
(c) Government set up the National Informatics Centre (NIC) in 1975-76 to 
provide computerization support to the Central Government Departments. The 
role of the NIC was extended in 1985 to the State Governments, including 
District Headquarters. 
The NIC has established a nationwide Information and Communications 
Technologies Network (NICNET) - with gateway nodes in all Central Government 
Departments, State/UT Secretariats and about 600 Districts. 
The NIC has developed many E-Governanc e applications in the area of 
Judiciary, Agriculture, Rural Development, Land Records, Transport, Passport 
Services, Sales Tax, Customs and Excise, Property Registration, Civil 
Pension/Social Welfare Pension, Public Grievances, Accounts etc. and these 
applications are already operational. 
(d) The adoption of E-Governance is an ongoing process in all the 
States. According to, The India: E-Readiness Assessment Report 2003', 
the States of Andhra Pradesh, Karnataka, Tamil Nadu and Gujarat have 
emerged as leading States in the country based on the index of E- 
governance.

. 1975. SHRI A. VIJAYA RAGHAVAN: Wi ll the Minister  of CONSUMER

(d) if so, the details of the "hunger hot spots" of the country identified as a

Disinvestment in Jessop Company Limited 
1982. SHRI GAYA SINGH:  
SHRI V.V. RAGHAVAN: 
Will the Minister of DISINVESTMENT be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that th e Kolkata High Court has cleared the 
disinvestment of Jessop Company Limited; and 
(b) if so, the details thereof? 
120 

[7 August, 2003] RAJYA SABHA 
THE MINISTER OF DISINVESTMENT (SHRI ARUN SHOURIE): (a) Yes, 
Sir. 
(b) Jessop & Co. Ltd. Staff Association filed a writ petition in the Kolkata 
High Court against the decision of the Government to disinvest 72% equity in 
Jessop and Co. Ltd. The Single Judge Bench of Kolkata High Court, in March 
2003, upheld that Jessop and Co. Ltd. do es not fall within  the category of 
'strategic sector and hence, that the Government of India can disinvest majority 
stake in Jessop and Co. Ltd.The Hon'ble Single Judge Bench however, set aside 
the decision of the Government to sell 72% equity to M/s. Ruia Cotext Ltd. 
(consortium) on certain procedural issues. Against the above judgement of the 
Kolkata High Court, Government of India filed an appeal before the Division 
Bench of the Kolkata High Court in May 2003.This appeal was disposed off by 
the Division Bench of Kolkata High Court vide their judgement dated 8.7.2003. 
The Division Bench in its judgement has upheld that Jessop and Co. Ltd. does 
not fall within the category of 'strategic sector and hence, that the Government 
of India can divest 72% equity in Jessop and Co. Ltd. The Division Bench also 
approved the sale of 72% equity in favour of M/s Ruia Cotex Ltd. (consortium) 
and concluded that the process and the procedures followed by Government 
of India were transparent.The Division Bench of Kolkata High Court rejected the 
prayer for stay of the judgement so ught by the Jessop and Co. Ltd. Staff 
Association. Jessop and Co. Ltd. Staff Association has filed a Special Leave 
Petition (SLP) before the Hon'ble Supr eme Court. No stay has been granted 
by the Supreme Court.

Support to India's cause against cross border terrorism 
1985. SHRI LALIT SURI: Will the Mi nister of EXTERNAL AFFAIRS be 
pleased to state: 
(a) whether there was any significant indication to help India's cause against 
cross border terrorism by Pakistan during the recent discussions of Deputy 
Prime Minister with the President of United States of America and the Prime 
Minister of United Kingdom; and 
(b) what follow up action is being taken by Government to help India's cause 
on the issue? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF EXTERNAL AFFAIRS 
(SHRI DIGVIJAY SINGH): (a) The U.S. President and the U.K. Prime Minister 
conveyed to the Deputy Prime Minister, during his visit to USA and UK in June 
2003; that they would cont inue to press Pakistan to fulfil its commitments on 
crossborder terrorism. 
(b) Government believes that Indi a is fully capable of combating 
crossborder terrorism on its own. At t he same time, Government continues its 
purposive engagement with the international community, which has led to 
widespread international recognition of Pakistan's responsibility to take steps 
for bringing an end to crossborder terrorism in India. 
131 

RAJYA SABHA [7 August, 2003] 
Pak failure to stop terrorism 
†1986. SHRIMATI MAYA SINGH: W ill the Minister of EXTERNAL 
AFFAIRS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that Presid ent of Pakistan has categorically stated 
during the visit to his country by the leaders from abroad and during his own 
visit to foreign countries, that he cannot stop terrorism going on in Jammu and 
Kashmir, completely; 
(b) if so, whether it would adversely affect the peace talk to be held 
between the two countries; and 
(c) if so, Government's reaction thereto? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF EXTERNAL AFFAIRS 
(SHRI DIGVIJAY SINGH): (a) Contrary to  facts, the President of Pakistan, 
General Musharraf, has from time to  time claimed inter alia that nothing was 
happening across the Line of Control, Pakistan had done all it could, or 
suggested that Pakistani State or agencies were not behind the terrorists acting 
against India. 
(b) and (c) President Musharraf's comments are clearly unhelpful in the 
context of Prime Minister's initiative to establish trust and confidence in India-
Pakistan relations. 
Government have made it clear that creation of conducive atmosphere for 
a sustained dialogue necessarily required an end to cross border terrorism 
and dismantling of the infrastructure of support to terrorism in Pakistan.

Break-through due to step by step approach with Pakistan 
1988. PROF. M. SANKARALINGAM: W ill the Minister of EXTERNAL 
AFFAIRS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether step by step approach of India with Pakistan has been on for 
quite some time; 
133 

RAJYA SABHA [7 August, 2003] 
(b) if so, the break-through made in this direction; 
(c) whether the said approach is playing any role in the engagement 
between India and Pakistan; and 
(d) if so, the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF EXTERNAL AFFAIRS 
(SHRI DIGVIJAY SINGH): (a) to (d) Prime Minister had, on April 18, 2003, 
once again extended the hand of friendship to Pakistan. In his statement in 
Parliament on May 2, he had announced the decision to appoint a High 
Commissioner to Pakistan and to restore civil aviation links on a reciprocal 
basis. It had also been made clear that India would pursue a step-by-step 
approach to normalisation of links and that  creating conditions conducive to 
sustained dialogue necessarily required an  end to cross-border infiltration and 
dismantling of the infrastructure of support to terrorism in Pakistan. Subsequently, 
on May 26, Government indicated its willingness for the resumption of Delhi-
Lahore bus service. 
Following Prime Minister's initiative both countries have appointed High 
Commissioners. The Delhi-Lahore bus service has been resumed with effect 
from July 11. Technical level discussions for resumption of civil aviation are 
scheduled to be held on August 27-28,2003. Both sides have released prisoner. 
There have also been important exchanges in the context of business, cultural 
and people-to-people contacts. 
India is committed to resolving all outstanding issues with Pakistan 
peacefully through direct bilateral dialogue in the spirit of Simla Agreement and 
Lahore Declaration. Government intends to proceed with present approach of 
step-by-step normalization of diplomatic and other links. Further steps would 
be considered based on the progress made, and confidence generated.

tranfer of employees.

Ministry that all pendencies would be  cleared in specific time frame and 
maintained at zero level. However, this has not happended and pendencies 
are instead increasing. It may be further mentioned t hat AIPEA in disregard of 
the Conduct Rules has gone on strike and go-slow and other forms of agitation. 
In addition to such action taken by AI PEA being illegal, the agitations of AIPEA

Objectives of National Population Policy 
2045. SHRI S.S. AHLUWALIA: Will the PRIME MINISTER be pleased to 
state: 
(a) whether the medium-term objective set in the National Population Policy 
(NPP) to achieve the Total Fertility Rate (TFR) at 2.1 level by 2010 would 
restrict our population to 111.90 crore by 2011, whereas, the Planning 
Commission target to restrict population growth during 2001-11 to 16.2 per 
cent would result in a population size exceeding 119 core; 
(b) what such higher target of Planning Commission, which might also 
negate the long-term objective in the NP P for a stable population by 2045, is 
attributable to; and 
(c) whether Planning Commission has drawn the target in 
consultation with National Commission on population? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF PLANNING (SHRI 
SATYABRATA MOOKHERJEE): (a) to (c) The medium-term objective of the 
National Population Policy (NPP) 2000 is to achieve the Total Fertility Rate 
(TFR) 2.1 by 2010. The population projections used in the NPP document were 
based on the 1991 census data. Assuming that the TFR 2.1 would be achieved 
by the year 2010, the NPP projected the population for 2010 at 110.07 crore. 
However, the 2001 census has shown that the actual population had exceeded 
the projections made in the NPP. The Planning Commission has set a target to 
bring down decadal population growth to 16.2% between 2001 and 2011. This 
target is consistent with the medium-t erm and long-term obje ctives set in the 
NPP. If this target is achieved, the population of the country will be around 
119.3 crore by the year 2011. The Tenth Plan demographic targets have been 
made in consultation with the National Commission 
180 

[7 August, 2003] RAJYA SABHA 
on Population and after taking into consideration the actual population growth 
recorded by census 2001.

Rehabilitation of SSI units 
2072. SHRI K. RAMA MOHANA RAO: Will the Minister of SMALL SCALE 
INDUSTRIES be pleased to state: 
(a) the details of steps that have been taken to offset the trend of 
sickness in the SSI sector; and 
(b) the steps that have been taken to rehabilitate SSI units in the 
country? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN TH E MINISTRY OF SMALL SCALE 
INDUSTRIES (SHRI TAPAN SIKDAR): (a) and (b) The number of sick Small 
Scale Industries (SSIs) has declined from 3,06,221 as at the end of March, 
1999 to 1,77,336 as at the end of March, 2002 as per the latest data compiled 
by the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) from Scheduled Commercial Banks. 
The Government is fully seized of the problem of industrial sickness 
amogst the SSI units and has taken various steps to facilitate timely 
identification and rehabilitation of potentially viable sick industries including 
institutional mechanism in the form of State-level Inter-Institutional 
Committees, Special Rehabilitation Ce lls in banks and State Financial 
Institutions. Elaborate guidelines have been issued by the Reserve Bank of 
India for extending rehabilitation assistance to eligible units. Further, based on 
the recommendations of the Working Group set up under the Chairmanship of 
Shri S.S. Kohli, the RBI has drawn up re vised guidelines for rehabilitation of 
sick SSI units, which include inter-alia change in the definition of sick SSI 
units, norms for deciding on their viability, concessional finance, etc. The RBI 
has circulated the revised guidelines on 16th January, 2002 to all the 
scheduled commercial banks for implementation. 
203

Recession in SSI sector 
2073. SHRI PARMESHWAR KUMAR AGAR WALLA: Will the Minister of 
SMALL SCALE INDUSTRIES be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government are aware that many small scale industrial units 
are facing unprecedented recession; and 
(b) if so, what steps are taken by Government to revive small scale units 
and to boost their performance? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF SMALL SCALE 
INDUSTRIES (SHRI TAPAN SIKDAR): (a) While the annual growth rate of Small 
Scale Industries (SSIs) Sector declined from 8.23 per cent in 2000-01 to 6.08 
per cent in 2001-02, the same is estima ted to have increased to 7.41 per cent 
in 2002-03. The downtrend in 2001-02 could be partly due to overall 
recessionary trend in the industrial sector. 
(b) To strengthen and enhance the competitiveness of the SSI Sector, both 
domestically and globally, the Government has taken various measures, which 
include enhancement of working capital limit computed on the basis of minimum 
of 20% of annual projected.turnover from Rs. 4 crore to Rs. 5 crore, 
enhancement in composite loan limit from Rs. 10 lakhs to Rs. 25 lakhs, raising 
of project cost limit under National Equity Fund Scheme from Rs. 25 lakhs to Rs. 
50 lakhs, revision in eligible loan limit for coverage under Credit Guarantee 
Scheme from Rs. 10 lakhs to Rs. 25 lakhs, introduction of Laghu Udyami Credit 
Card (LUCC) Scheme, issuance of revised guidelines for rehabilitation of sick 
SSI units and revival of potentially viable units, by the Reserve Bank of India on 
16th January, 2002, etc. Further, in accordance with the announcement made 
in the Union Budget 2003-04, the Indian Banks' Association has advised all its 
member banks to adopt an interest rate bank of 2 per cent above and below 
Prime Lending Rate (PLR) as announced by  the State Bank of India. Banks 
have also agreed to further raise the composite loan limit from Rs. 25 lakhs to 
Rs. 50 lakhs.

GOVERNMENT BILLS 
The Central Vigilance Commission Bill, 2003  , 
 SHRI A. VIJAYA RAGHAVAN (Kerala) : Mr. Chairman, Sir. we have 
started this discussion yesterday onwards. It is a very serious matter. After 
discussion in the Subject Committee, this Bill came up for discussion in this 
House. According to the World Economic Survey, both in terms of corruption 
and dishonesty of officials, out of 49 count ries. India's rank is 45". In 1999, in 
international ranking for transparency, India's rank was 73 ' amongst 99 
countries. The lack of transparency provi des an opportunity to public servants 
to extracting bribes and misleading citizens, who have to transact business 
with them. Sir. certainly, India's size of parallel economy is estimated at 40 per 
cent of the GDP which provides a fe rtile ground for corruption. Equally 
important, the corrupt face little deterrence in this country. There are 
enormous delays in the pros ecution of cases in courts. What is worse, the 
conviction rate is hardly six per cent  in criminal cases. Corruption is anti-
national. This Bill came immediately after this hawala scam. The hawala scam 
showed that the anti-national milit ants were sending money from abroad 
through hawala. Corruption is anti-poor, since the resources meant for poverty 
alleviation schemes get siphoned off by  corrupt bureaucrats and politicians. 
Corruption is anti-development. It was demonstrated by the experiences of 
1997 in the East-Asian economy. What happened? There was a total collapse 
of the economy because of the involvement of corrupt bureaucracy.   That 
experience is there in the South- 
217 

RAJYA SABHA [7 August, 2 003] 
East Asian countries. Sir, we are discussing a very serious matter. It may 
repeat recur in our country. If this condition prevails, it may recur in our 
country. It is against the basic foundati ons of democracy. It also increases 
poverty, subverts the financial system and undermines the legitimacy of the 
State. Thus, corruption is anti-p oor, anti-development, anti-growth, anti-
investment and inequitable. The cost of  corruption to a nation is very high. 
There is a perception that  corruption begins at t he top. Because of that 
perception, we have to refer to this Bill. 
With regard to CVC, we have had so many experiences. Our CVC, 
when it was a one-member CVC, took initiatives to curb corruption and 
intervened to identify the corrupt officials and the corrupt bureaucrats. What 
has happened? The former CVC started a website which published the names 
of senior officers who were charged with  violating the conduct rules. On that 
website, he had displayed the names of se nior officials of the Government of 
India, including the IAS and IPS office rs. That caused a mild furore in the 
media. One of the IAS Officers' Associat ions passed a resolution against the 
CVC stating that the pub lication of a name on t he website could bias the 
process of a departmental inquiry. 
(THE DEPUTY CHAIRMAN in the Chair) 
Then, the CVC website came out with  some other report. As per that 
report, in the banking sector, over a dozen departments, especially loans and 
advance wings of six banks have been identified as corruption-prone despite 
the fact that the adminis tration has launched several preventive measures to 
check the menace. In the banking sector, the CVC has named certain 
departments of State Bank of Patiala,  Canara Bank, State Bank of Indore, 
Syndicate Bank and Bank of Saurashtra as extremely corruption prone. 
With regard to the DDA, the CVC asked them to keep the suspected 
officers under surveillance and prepare a list of officers of doubtful integrity. 
Now, what had happened? Even after the CVC had given such an instruction, 
there was a scam in the DDA! Even if the CVC gives some instructions and 
expresses its apprehensions, no action is taken. The CVC has also written, at 
least, three letters, on June 28, July 7 and July 15 of 2002, to banks, asking 
them to comply with the CVC's in structions and the CVO's recommendation 
for penalty and launching criminal proceedings against the corrupt officials, 
but there was no response from the Administration.

[7 August, 2003] RAJYA SABHA 
Madam, you are also aware of the ar rest of Mr. B.P. Verma, Chairman 
of the Central Board of Excise and Customs (CBSC)--an agency that provides 
the Central Government with half the revenue to keep itself running; that 
showed how the system has for years been rewarding the corrupt with 
promotion and career advancement. 
Madam, the value of assets owned by Mr. Verma was nearly Rs.40 
crores. He was on a vigilance watch-fist for some years, but not miss his 
opportunities to rise in the hierarchy of  the India Revenue Service. This is the 
situation. The top official who was co llecting half of the revenue was under 
surveillance, and he had been promoted! Madam, we had that experience. 
Before that, the CVC, Mr. Vittal, was also informed about the background of this 
fellow. Despite that, his name has been cleared even by the PMO as the Chief 
of the CVC. This is the situation! In this  situation, naturally, this country needs 
an enactment to provide more strength to  the CVC. That is why, there is an 
intervention from the apex Court. Now, the Bill is in front of us. Naturally, I have 
to support some aspects of this Bill which is going to provide more powers to 
the CVC. Here, Madam, we have given a st atutory status to the CVC; it is a 
good step. Similarly, we have decided to  increase the number of members in 
the CVC. Naturally, this also would be a step forward. Shri B.P. Jeevan Reddy, 
the Law Commission Chairman, has expr essed the view that the CVC should 
be a multi-member body with persons from specialised fields like finance, law, 
administration and vigilance. This would strengthen the CVC. In this Bill, we 
are making provisions for strengthening t he CVC.   I am supporting both these 
clauses.
